title: Gateway contradiction
briefing: The workstation can reach its switch but cannot contact a server on another subnet.

evidence.label: The workstation has address 192.168.10.17/24.
Its configured gateway does not match 192.168.10.1.
The server is accessible from another subnet.
A physical cable failure was blamed without a link test.

conclusions: Incorrect default gateway is a supported diagnosis.
The office firewall was certainly compromised.
A lost packet proves the server was deleted.
feedback: This supports a routing misconfiguration, not malicious activity.

title: Unlisted segment
briefing: The diagram omits a monitoring uplink from the recorded switch inventory.

evidence.label: Printed topology lists office and service segments.
Switch inventory includes an uplink absent from the paper diagram.
MIRROR appears in a port description.
An anonymous report calls the uplink a secret tunnel.

conclusions: The diagram is incomplete; the purpose of the uplink remains uncertain.
The uplink is definitely an attacker command channel.
Every omitted connection means an active incident.
feedback: Describe the discrepancy without assigning intent.

title: Unusual resolution
briefing: A suspicious hostname is queried by a training workstation.

evidence.label: A DNS query requests mirror.training.invalid.
The synthetic resolver returns 198.51.100.53.
No packet provides the user intention behind the request.
A message claims all DNS requests are spying.

conclusions: The DNS resolution occurred; user intent cannot be inferred from it alone.
The hostname proves sensitive files were uploaded.
The query confirms the user is a Directorate agent.
feedback: Resolve protocol facts before narrative claims.

title: Silent intermediary
briefing: A traceroute stops displaying responses at an intermediate hop.

evidence.label: The route tool sees a response from the first gateway.
The next router did not send a visible TTL-expired reply.
The final service responds to another test.
An analyst calls the unresponsive hop destroyed.

conclusions: An intermediate router may filter diagnostic replies while forwarding traffic.
All packets stopped permanently at that router.
The ISP secretly changed the destination.
feedback: No ICMP reply is not equivalent to a confirmed forwarding failure.

title: Capture discrepancy
briefing: A published packet summary omits the three-frame DNS transaction.

evidence.label: The supplied capture contains a three-frame DNS sequence.
The signed summary does not mention DNS queries.
A capture hash identifies the reviewed fixture.
A forum post blames a particular employee.

conclusions: The summary is incomplete relative to this capture.
A particular employee definitely altered it.
The capture reveals private HTTPS content.
feedback: The discrepancy warrants review, not an automatic attribution.

title: Unregistered service
briefing: A loopback-only inventory discovers a TCP listener.

evidence.label: The authorized training target is 127.0.0.1.
A temporary TCP service reports open during the test.
The illustrative inventory did not list that service.
An open port is called a confirmed breach.

conclusions: A reachable service is exposed within the approved lab scope.
The host has conclusively been compromised.
A port scan extracts private credentials.
feedback: Recommend inventory review; an open port is not proof of exploitation.

title: Training credential
briefing: A deliberately weak synthetic password is found by a local auditing tool.

evidence.label: The test hash was generated for this lesson only.
A short training wordlist matched the fixture.
The test vault contains no real user accounts.
One match proves every account uses the same password.

conclusions: The training credential is weak against the demonstrated audit.
Real company passwords have all been cracked.
Hashing and encryption are the same.
feedback: Explain adaptive password hashing and defense in depth.

title: Portal authorization
briefing: The synthetic MIRROR portal serves case records by object identifier.

evidence.label: The learner changes the case identifier in a local GET request.
The local service responds without checking object-level access.
Only fictional training data exists in this service.
Someone claims every web application has this defect.

conclusions: The training service lacks an object-level authorization check.
Every website can be breached by changing a URL.
The browser must always authenticate the server itself.
feedback: Authorization needs to be enforced on the server.

title: Conflicting logs
briefing: Two independent records disagree about MIRROR metadata.

evidence.label: MI-07 records MIRROR metadata at the incident time.
IS-21 denies that the metadata exists.
Timestamps establish an ordering but not a motive.
The first hypothesis names a guilty party without verification.

conclusions: There is an evidence discrepancy requiring independent corroboration.
The discrepancy proves deliberate deception by a named person.
All logs must have been fabricated.
feedback: Correlate records; avoid definitive attribution based on conflict alone.

title: The disclosure choice
briefing: The final dossier is technically supported but contains sensitive context.

evidence.label: The dossier states observations separately from inferences.
Some bystanders are not implicated by the technical evidence.
Independent review can evaluate the claims with safeguards.
A leak promises absolute proof without source verification.

conclusions: Proportionate, evidence-based disclosure should protect affected people.
Publish every record, including unrelated private information.
Destroy the case materials to avoid conflict.
feedback: A strong technical case still requires an ethical decision.
